title: Fast-track UK settlement proposed for high earning dental professionals
html:
Eligible dental professionals could access UK settlement within three or five years under government proposals for a new public service pathway, though it is unclear which job roles fall under the new route.

The government announced the new routes to permanent right to remain in the UK in its A fairer pathway to settlement report, which listed a total of five pathways.

‘Dental practitioners’ are specifically named as eligible for the permanent five-year public service route, though a spokesperson for the Home Office was unable to confirm which GDC registrant titles fall into this category, stating that more information would be available shortly.

However, eligibility for two of the fast track public service pathways is dependant on the following minimum income thresholds:

The earnings-based five-year route would require applicants to earn at least £50,271 in three of the previous five years. However, eligible dental practitioners could qualify separately after five years in a qualifying public-sector role paid on national pay scales, regardless of whether they met that salary threshold.

Time spent in the UK on student or graduate visas would no longer count towards settlement through long residence under the proposals.

How is settlement changing for dental professionals earning less than £50k?

The government also plans to increase the period that lower-skilled health workers must wait for settled status from five to 10 years, applying to jobs that do not require a university degree such as dental nursing. This replaces previous plans for the period to increase to 15 years, which were met with significant backlash.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: ‘[Settlement] is granted near automatically, largely on the basis of time served. It is this government’s view that this is insufficient. The right to settle should instead reflect a lasting commitment to this country, demonstrated through contribution, integration and
respect for our laws and values.’

Some healthcare workers in roles below degree level on national pay scales would retain a five-year settlement route if they arrived before publication of the immigration white paper in May 2025 and met their visa requirements.

Neil Carmichael, executive chair of the Association of Dental Groups (ADG), called for clarity on the status of overseas dental professionals. He said: ‘The value skilled health workers bring to our NHS teams is vast. This is particularly important for dentistry as we struggle to fill the workforce gap. ADG dental groups are extremely grateful for the hard work international dentists are giving in supporting the provision of dental care in the UK, and we must treat our dental workforce who move to the uk from overseas well and with respect.’

All settlement routes will carry stricter baseline requirements: B2 English, a Life in the UK exam, no outstanding government debt, a clean criminality record, and no access to specified public funds in the preceding five years.

Are there other routes that allow overseas dental professionals to practise in the UK?

This comes as Home Office figures have revealed that sponsored visa grants for overseas dental nurses had fallen by 95% after the government removed the role from the skilled worker route.

Practice owner David Chong Kwan said closing the route had been a ‘disaster’. David has trained dental nurses within his own practice but does not believe that domestic training has produced enough experienced people to meet demand.

With the vast majority of dental nurses to be excluded from both the skilled worker visa and accelerated settlement, routes into UK dental nursing from overseas are continuing to narrow.
